literal: the original substrate, the natural state; from pra- + √kṛ 'to make' (literally 'that from which makings proceed')

definition_claims.text: In the reviewed Sāṅkhya passage, *prakṛti* is the non-conscious productive causal order contrasted with *puruṣa*; it is not merely a synonym for the visible world.

The term marks the side of change, embodiment, and causal transformation, in contrast with *puruṣa*. Classical Sāṅkhya uses that distinction to explain experience and release without making consciousness itself a product of material change.

Vedāntic use cannot be presumed to retain Sāṅkhya's independent material principle. In Rāmānuja's opening account, the conscious and non-conscious order is qualified by and dependent on the inner-controlling Brahman; the shared vocabulary therefore carries a different dependence-claim.

claims.text: In the Sāṅkhya account, the manifest and the primal source are marked by the three *guṇas*, while *puruṣa* is defined in contrast to that non-conscious, productive order. *Prakṛti* is therefore the causal side of a world that can develop bodies, sense capacities, and cognitive instruments without turning consciousness itself into an effect of matter.

The text describes an evolution from *prakṛti* through *mahat* toward the elements and their objects, while also saying that the activity of *pradhāna* is for the sake of the *puruṣa*’s release. This is why *prakṛti* is not simply a synonym for the visible world: it is the causal matrix whose activity makes experience and discrimination possible.

exposition_sections.title: Why Vedāntic reuse changes the question

claims.text: Vedāntic authors can inherit the causal vocabulary without granting *prakṛti* independent ultimacy. Rāmānuja’s opening description makes the conscious and non-conscious orders qualifications of Viṣṇu, and his inner-controller account treats the material order as dependent on Brahman. The enduring dispute is therefore not whether there is embodiment and causal transformation, but whether the material principle is independent, a dependent mode, or an appearance under a different ontology.

invariant_definition: *Prakṛti* is the fabric of material manifestation: the unmanifest causal substrate woven from the three *guṇa*s, whose disturbed equilibrium unfolds as *mahat*, *ahaṅkāra*, the subtle elements, the gross elements, the body, and the cognitive apparatus. The image of a fabric is explanatory, not a claim that Sanskrit uses a modern physical textile metaphor: the *guṇa*s are the constitutive strands or qualities by which Sāṅkhya analyzes this material order. The term therefore does not mean 'nature' in the modern contrast between nature and culture. It names the causal matrix presupposed by embodiment, *saṃsāra*, and the whole debate over whether the effect pre-exists in the cause. In Sāṅkhya it is *avyakta* and *pradhāna*: unconscious, eternal, and independent of *puruṣa* even while acting for *puruṣa*'s experience and liberation. Vedānta takes over the causal grammar but refuses that independence. *Prakṛti* is then redescribed as *māyā*, *acit*, external *śakti*, or dependent material principle under *brahman* or Īśvara. Across these redescriptions one point remains stable: the body, senses, pleasure-pain apparatus, and inner instrument belong to the *prakṛti* side, not to consciousness as such. The disputes concern whether *prakṛti* is ultimate or dependent, whether its transformations are fully real or only *vyāvahārika*, and whether the Lord stands to it as controller, substrate, or merely apparent possessor of an *upādhi*.

school_framing.shared_core: *Prakṛti* names **the materially manifesting principle: the *upādāna* of evolved form**, marked by the three *guṇas* (*Sāṅkhya-Kārikā* 11–13). Sāṅkhya gives the paradigm definition; Yoga inherits it; Vedāntic schools then reinterpret *prakṛti* as *brahman*'s real or modal power, not an independent substance.
school_framing.register_axes_note: **Real disagreement** (AF1) between Sāṅkhya (*prakṛti* *svatantra*, independent of *puruṣa*) and Vedāntic schools (*prakṛti* either *brahman*'s *śakti* or *brahman*'s *aṃśa*). Same M-register, same scope-inside ('the material principle'), opposing claims on its dependence-status.

per_school.definition: *Prakṛti* is the independent unconscious root cause (*pradhāna*, *avyakta*) constituted by the three *guṇa*s. Because Sāṅkhya is *satkārya-vādin*, the manifest world is an actual evolution of what was already present in *prakṛti* in unmanifest form. Its disequilibrium issues in *mahat*, *ahaṅkāra*, the *tanmātras*, the elements, and the body-mind complex. Yoga accepts the same ontology but subordinates it to the practical isolation of *puruṣa* through discriminative knowledge.

*Prakṛti* is admitted as the material-causal order only at the *vyāvahārika* level and is functionally identified with *māyā*. The Sāṅkhya thesis that *pradhāna* is an independent ultimate cause is rejected. Body, senses, and *antaḥkaraṇa* belong to *prakṛti*; *ātman* does not. Hence bondage is explained through *upādhi* and *adhyāsa*, not through any real modification of *brahman*. *Prakṛti* is thus indispensable to the appearance of the world but not ultimately self-standing.

*Prakṛti* is real *acit*: one of the eternal reals constituting the body of *brahman*. It is dependent, not independent, but its transformations are real. Rāmānuja therefore accepts the causal work that Sāṅkhya assigns to *prakṛti* while denying that it could stand apart from the Lord. Bound embodiment, the senses, and the changing world are all genuine transformations of *prakṛti* governed from within by Nārāyaṇa.

In Tattva-vāda (Dvaita), *Prakṛti* is a real dependent reality under Viṣṇu's control, distinct from both Viṣṇu and the plurality of *jīva*s. Madhva accepts the reality of the material order and its causal efficacy while rejecting any claim that it is self-moving or self-grounding. Its transformations are real, but they occur only under the will of the unique *svatantra*, Viṣṇu. The difference between *prakṛti*, *jīva*, and Lord is therefore not pedagogical but ontological.

*Prakṛti* is the material side of Kṛṣṇa's external power, often described as *guṇa-māyā* within the broader *bahiraṅgā-śakti*. It is real and causally effective, yet radically dependent on Bhagavān. What binds the *jīva* is not only residence in a material world but residence in this external energy rather than in the Lord's internal *svarūpa-śakti*.

translator_note: 'Nature' is the standard lazy gloss and is usually wrong. It imports a modern nature-versus-culture contrast and suggests forests, animals, or the non-human environment. *Prakṛti* instead names the material-causal substrate presupposed by Sāṅkhya causality, guṇa theory, and embodiment. 'Matter' is closer, but even that can import post-Cartesian or physicalist assumptions foreign to the Sanskrit debates. In most contexts the safest practice is to leave *prakṛti* untranslated and specify whether the school treats it as independent root cause, dependent *acit*, or external divine *śakti*.
